questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14041963/assets/74850221ee168c6911ee5b6c319d2128f67149f81790528940822e253905fc0f.png)

The function $y=f(x)$ above is continuous on the interval $[-5,3]$ and differentiable on  $(-5,3).$  What is the missing part of the sentence in the statement below?

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c\in (-5,3)$ such that $\text{_______}\,.$ *
questions.worked_solution:
Given that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on  $(a,b)$, the mean value theorem states the following:

*There exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that*

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

In our case, we have $a=-5$ and $b=3.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(3)-f(-5)}{3-(-5)} \\  & =\frac{-2-2}{3+5} \\  & =\frac{-4}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

 *The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c\in (-5,3)$ such that ${f}^{′}(c)=-\frac{1}{2}.$*

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.problem:
Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for 
 $f(x)=-3\sqrt{x}+2$ on the interval $[0,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[0,2]$ and differentiable on $(0,2),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (0,2)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0} \\  & =\frac{(-3\sqrt{2}+2)-(-3\sqrt{0}+2)}{2} \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-3\sqrt{x}+2)=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{c}}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2\sqrt{c}} & =-\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{c}} & =\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{c} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ c & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for  $f(x)=3{x}^{2}+x-2$ on the interval $[-1,2].$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,2]$ and differentiable on $(-1,2),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (-1,2)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=-1$ and $b=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(2)-f(-1)}{2-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot {2}^{2}+2-2)-(3\cdot (-1)^{2}+(-1)-2)}{2+1} \\  & =\frac{12-0}{3} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+x-2)=6x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=6c+1.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}6c+1 & =4 \\ 6c & =3 \\ c & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for 
 $f(x)={x}^{2}-2x+5$ on the interval $[1,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[1,4]$ and differentiable on $(1,4),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (1,4)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=1$ and $b=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1} \\  & =\frac{({4}^{2}-2\cdot 4+5)-({1}^{2}-2\cdot 1+5)}{3} \\  & =\frac{13-4}{3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-2x+5)=2x-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=2c-2.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2c-2 & =3 \\ 2c & =5 \\ c & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

First, notice that the function $h(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,3]$ and differentiable on $(-1,3),$ so it satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $p(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,3]$ but has a corner point at $x=2.$ Hence, $p(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=2,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(-1,3).$ Therefore, $p(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $r(x)$  has a vertical asymptote at $x=-1.$ Hence, $r(x)$  is not continuous on $[-1,3].$ Therefore, $r(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $t(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,3]$ but has a corner point at $x=0.$ Hence, $t(x)$ is not differentiable at $x=0,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(-1,3).$ Therefore, $t(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,1]?$

- $f(x)=2|x|$
- $g(x)=|x-1|$
- $h(x)=|x+1|$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,1],$ the function must be continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x)=2|x|$ is continuous on $[-1,1],$ but it has a corner in $x=0.$ Hence, it is not differentiable at $x=0,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(-1,1).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)=|x-1|$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1)$ because it is equivalent to $p(x)=1-x$ over the given interval. Therefore, $g(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem. Note that the graph of $y=g(x)$ has a corner point at $x=1$ but this point does not lie inside $(-1,1).$

- The function $h(x)=|x+1|$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1)$ because it is equivalent to $p(x)=x+1$ over the given interval. Therefore, $h(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem. Note that the graph of $y=h(x)$ has a corner point at $x=-1$ but this point does not lie inside $(-1,1).$

Therefore, only functions II and III satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[-1,1].$

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,3]?$

- $p(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$
- $q(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$
- $r(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(|x-1|)$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,3],$ the function must be continuous on $[1,3]$ and differentiable on $(1,3).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $p(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[1,3]$ and differentiable on $(1,3).$ Therefore, $p(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $q(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is continuous and differentiable on $(1,\infty ).$ Given that it is not defined at $x=1,$ $q(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $r(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,1)\cup (1,\infty ).$ Given that it is not defined at $x=1,$ $r(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only function I satisfies the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,3].$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Completing the Mean Value Theorem Statement From the Graph of a Function
canonical_examples.problem:
The function $y=f(x)$ below is continuous on $[-1,4]$ and differentiable on $(-1,4).$  Complete the sentence below.

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c \in (-1,4)$ such that $\_\_\_\_\_\_ \, .$ *

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14041963/assets/5672cc68e55078623f34f01650d3e82bd3cee62e6ca97fabcd2287f2a865501a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given that $f(x)$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b),$ the mean value theorem states the following:

*There exists a point $c \in (a,b)$ such that
$f'(c) = \dfrac {f(b) - f(a)} {b-a}.$*

In our case, we have $a = -1$ and $b=4,$ so the above statement becomes 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(4)-f(-1)}{4-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{6-2}{4+1} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $c \in (-1,4)$ such that* $f'(c) =\dfrac {4}{5}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
canonical_examples.problem: Find the values of $c$ that satisfy the mean value theorem for  $f(x) = x^2$ on the interval $[0,2].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$  is a polynomial, so it is continuous on $[0,2]$ and differentiable on $(0,2).$ 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c \in (0,2)$ such that 

$$
f'(c)   = \dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=0$ and $b=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-(0)} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{2}-{0}^{2}}{2} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})=2x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
f'(c) = 2c.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2c & =2 \\ c & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Functions Presented Graphically That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[−2,2]?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14041963/assets/e680c2e80874a4c2e8b4d31fcc7a6ba42a3c55fb7c6f559e42f3cd785b22e3ed.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-2,2],$ the function must be continuous on $[-2,2]$ and differentiable on $(-2,2).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function shown in diagram $\textrm{I}$ is continuous on $[-2,2]$ and differentiable on $(-2,2)$, so it satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem. Note that the sharp corners at $x=\pm 2$ are not in $(-2,2).$

- The function shown in diagram $\textrm{II}$ has a removable discontinuity at $x=-2.$ So it is not continuous on $[-2,2],$ and therefore it does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function shown in diagram $\textrm{III}$ is continuous on $[-2,2]$ and differentiable on $(-2,2),$ so it satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem. Note that although the function has a jump discontinuity at $x=-2,$ it is right-continuous at $x=-2.$

- The function shown in diagram $\textrm{IV}$ is continuous on $[−2,2]$ but has a vertical tangent at $x=0.$ So, it is not differentiable at $x=0,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(−2,2).$  Therefore, it does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

In conclusion, only diagrams $\textrm{I}$ and $\textrm{III}$ show functions that satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-2,2].$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Functions That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,1]?$

- $f(x)= 3^{x} - 1$

- $g(x)= x^3 - x^2 + 1$

- $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,1],$ the function must be continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x) = 3^{x} - 1$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty, \infty).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)= x^3 - x^2 + 1$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty, \infty).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[0,1]$ and differentiable on $(0,1).$ Therefore, $g(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is not defined at $x = 0,$ hence, it is not continuous at 
$x = 0,$ and so it is not continuous on $[0,1].$ Therefore, $h(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only the functions I and II satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,1].$
